screens.title: DNS and Global Server Load Balancing
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll explore how the Domain Name System, the internet’s phonebook, becomes a decision point for global traffic. DNS starts as a simple mechanism to convert a human name into an IP address. When applications scale across regions, DNS can no longer remain static: we need Global Server Load Balancing, or GSLB, to route users to the best region based on location, latency, health, and capacity. You will learn why Round Robin DNS is insufficient for resilient, low-latency systems, and how GSLB algorithms like geo-location routing, latency-based routing, weighted routing, and failover behave in real deployments. We’ll also examine operational constraints: DNS caching, TTL tuning, and the importance of distributed health checks and multi-region application design. Through concrete examples and a small hands-on DNS zone fragment, you’ll see how a short TTL helps failover but increases DNS load, and why applications must be built to tolerate eventual consistency across regions. By the end, you should understand when GSLB is appropriate, what decisions it can automate, and what trade-offs remain for engineering teams. Consider how the system should behave if a whole region fails — that question will guide many design choices here.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › DNS & GSLB
DNS and Global Server Load Balancing
From name resolution to intelligent global routing for multi-region resilience.

In this chapter you will examine how DNS maps names to IPs, why Round Robin alone is not enough for modern distributed systems, and how GSLB adds intelligence: geo-based and latency-based routing, weights, and failover policies. We'll also look at TTL trade-offs and how health checks feed GSLB decisions.

Why this matters: when global outages, performance, or compliance constraints arise, the decisions DNS makes at the edge determine user experience and availability.

Explore Key Topics
DNS Basics
Name-to-IP resolution and Round Robin behavior.
GSLB Algorithms
GeoDNS, latency routing, weighting and failover.
Operational Trade-offs
TTL, cache propagation, health checks, and app design.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson
Understand DNS, why Round Robin falls short, and how GSLB chooses the best regional endpoint using health, location, latency, and policy.
Coming up
  • DNS basics and Round Robin
  • GSLB algorithms and examples
  • TTL, caching, and failover practice
Why it matters
Fast, reliable global routing reduces latency and prevents regional failures from causing widespread outages. DNS-level decisions are the first step.

You will also be able to define Global Server Load Balancing and list its common algorithms — geo-location routing, latency-based routing, weighted routing, and failover — and explain when each is appropriate. Finally, you will understand operational constraints such as TTL tuning, distributed health checks, and the application design changes required to operate across regions. Each objective ties a practical skill—like writing a conceptual DNS zone file or choosing a routing algorithm—to a reason why it matters in production. You will practice interpreting TTL trade-offs and plan for failover scenarios, which prepares you to make resilient architecture choices for global services.

screens.title: DNS: the internet’s phonebook
screens.narratorSegment: DNS is the hierarchical, distributed naming system that maps human-friendly domain names to numeric IP addresses. At the most basic level this mapping enables browsers and clients to find a server on the network. A traditional DNS record, such as an A record, lists the IP address for a domain and can include multiple IPs. That multiplicity is where DNS begins to resemble a simple load distributor: many resolvers will iterate through or rotate the IP list. A concrete example is a website that publishes two A records: one for a US region and one for a European region. A resolver doing Round Robin may hand out each IP in turn. But it’s crucial to understand that DNS itself does not open connections or verify health; it only supplies addresses. A common misconception is to expect DNS to provide instantaneous failover: because DNS responses are cached by resolvers and client systems, changes may take time to propagate. Therefore, while DNS is the first place you can influence where a user connects, it must be paired with monitoring and short TTLs when you need rapid changes. Think of DNS as the control plane that can steer traffic, but not as the runtime monitor that guarantees successful connections.

keyIdea.text: DNS maps names to IPs and can provide multiple addresses, but it does not perform health checks or manage live connections.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › DNS: the internet’s phonebook
Definition
DNS resolves domain names to IP addresses so clients can locate servers on the network.
Why it matters
  • It is the first decision point for routing external traffic.
  • Multiple A records give a basic form of distribution.
  • DNS is passive: it does not check server health or establish connections.
Concrete example
A domain lists a US IP and a Europe IP. Resolvers rotate answers, which can spread load, but they won’t remove unreachable IPs without operator action.
Common misconception
Expecting DNS to perform health checks and immediate failover is incorrect; DNS caching delays and lack of monitoring prevent that behavior.
Analogy
Think of DNS as a directory service that gives a phone number. It doesn't answer calls or check whether the number is currently in service.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

DNS resolves names and can list multiple IPs, but relying on it alone for dynamic failover is risky without health checks and low TTLs.

screens.title: Round Robin DNS and its behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Round Robin DNS is a simple technique where a domain publishes multiple A records and the DNS resolver returns IPs in a rotating order. This can distribute new clients across several servers or regions, and in small deployments it can provide a primitive form of load sharing. A concrete example is a small service listing two IPs for myapp. com; successive queries may result in alternating addresses. However, in real networks the effectiveness of Round Robin is limited because the resolvers and caching layers can hold answers for the TTL duration, so multiple clients behind the same resolver will receive the same IP for that period. Another important constraint is that DNS lacks active health checks: if one IP becomes unhealthy, DNS will continue to hand it out until records are changed and cached entries expire. A common misconception is that Round Robin balances load evenly across actual user connections; it balances DNS queries, not necessarily TCP sessions or request load. When you design global services, Round Robin can be a quick start, but you must plan for monitoring, short TTLs if you want rapid changes, and a strategy to remove unhealthy endpoints quickly. Consider also client-side retry behavior: clients that fail over may try another IP, but that adds latency and complexity for user experience.

keyIdea.text: Round Robin spreads DNS queries among listed IPs but does not ensure even request distribution or fast removal of unhealthy endpoints due to caching and lack of checks.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Round Robin DNS
Round Robin behavior
Multiple A records are served in rotation to distribute DNS queries across addresses.
How it works
  1. Authoritative DNS lists several A records for the same name.
  2. Resolvers return one IP per query, often rotating through the list.
  3. Clients connect to the returned IP; failed connections rely on client retries.
Limitations
  • Caching: resolvers and clients may hold the same IP for the TTL duration.
  • No health checks: DNS will hand out unhealthy IPs until records change.
  • Balances DNS queries, not necessarily requests or sessions.
Concrete scenario
A service lists two IPs in DNS. A resolver caches one address; many client machines behind that resolver will all connect to the same IP until the TTL expires—so load may be uneven in practice.
Check your understanding
If a server behind one of the published IPs fails, will Round Robin stop returning that IP? Why or why not?
Hint

DNS will continue returning it because it has no active health checks and cached responses persist until TTL expiry.

screens.title: Why traditional DNS is insufficient
screens.narratorSegment: Traditional DNS's simplicity is also the source of its problems for dynamic, global systems. The first limitation is the absence of active health checks: authoritative DNS doesn't monitor the reachability of backend servers, so an IP that routes to a failed service continues to be handed out. A second limitation is pervasive caching: client devices, local resolvers, and intermediate resolvers store DNS answers for the TTL period. This means a change on the authoritative server can take minutes or hours to become effective worldwide if TTLs are large. A third shortcoming is lack of intelligence: vanilla DNS does not know client geography, real network latency, or server load; it simply returns configured addresses. To illustrate the operational impact, imagine a primary region failing during business hours. With high TTLs, many resolvers will still use cached primary IPs for the duration of the TTL, causing prolonged outages for those clients. A common mitigation is to reduce TTL values, but that increases DNS query volume and load on authoritative servers. The trade-offs are fundamental: faster propagation versus higher DNS traffic. Effective global routing requires a smarter control plane that monitors health, measures latency, and makes per-query decisions—this is precisely where GSLB fits in.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › DNS limitations
Core limitations of traditional DNS
No health checks
DNS doesn't monitor backend servers, so stale entries can point clients to downed services.
Caching and TTL
Resolvers and clients cache results for the TTL, causing propagation delays after updates.
Lack of intelligence
No concept of client location, server load, or measured latency in vanilla DNS responses.
Operational trade-off
Lowering TTL improves failover speed but increases DNS query load. You must balance rapid propagation with authoritative DNS capacity and cost.
Common mistake

Assuming DNS updates remove bad IPs instantly. Cached records keep clients pointing to the old IP until cache expiry.

screens.title: What is Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB)?
screens.narratorSegment: Global Server Load Balancing, or GSLB, extends DNS with intelligence and programmability to map clients to the best regional endpoint. A GSLB system acts as the authoritative DNS for your domain but instead of returning a static list of IPs, it makes per-query decisions based on inputs like client geolocation, recent latency measurements, server health, and configured weights. For example, when a client asks for your application's IP, the GSLB inspects the resolver’s source IP to infer location, consults health checks to ensure regions are healthy, and may consult latency metrics to pick the fastest region. The returned IP is typically the address of a regional load balancer rather than an application server, so the regional balancer handles intra-region distribution. A key benefit is that GSLB centralizes global routing logic while still using DNS as the delivery mechanism. A frequent misconception is that GSLB eliminates the need to design your application for multi-region operation; it does not. You still must handle data replication, session handling, and consistency across regions. GSLB simply helps direct traffic in a smarter way that improves latency and availability at the edge.

keyIdea.title: GSLB in one line
keyIdea.text: GSLB is an intelligent authoritative DNS that picks the best regional endpoint per query using health, location, latency, and policy.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What is GSLB?
GSLB defined
A smart authoritative DNS that selects the most appropriate regional IP per client query.
Inputs GSLB uses
  • Client resolver IP for geo-location
  • Distributed health checks for each region
  • Latency telemetry and configured weights
What it returns
An IP for a regional load balancer, chosen to optimize latency, availability, or policy goals.
Concrete example
A European user’s resolver queries the authoritative GSLB. The GSLB sees the resolver IP, verifies European region health, and returns the EU load balancer IP, reducing latency.
Misconception
GSLB helps routing but does not replace the need for multi-region application design like data replication and statelessness.

screens.title: GSLB routing algorithms overview
screens.narratorSegment: GSLB implementations commonly support several routing modes, each with different trade-offs. Geo-location-based routing maps client resolvers to the nearest region by IP-derived geography; it's simple and reduces distance-related latency, but it can be fooled by complex network paths. Latency-based routing measures or estimates network latency between clients and regions and routes to the lowest-latency endpoint; this can better reflect actual performance but requires accurate telemetry. Weighted routing assigns proportional traffic to regions based on configured weights, which is useful for capacity control and staged rollouts. Failover routing defines primary and secondary regions so that if a primary becomes unhealthy, traffic moves to the secondary automatically; this is critical for disaster recovery. Finally, IP-based routing maps specific client IP ranges to designated regions, often used for partners or internal networks. For example, a gaming company prioritizing minimal ping might choose latency-based routing, while a company wanting regional compliance controls might prefer geo-location routing. A misconception to avoid is treating these as mutually exclusive; many GSLB systems combine modes—geo for broad guidance and latency for fine-grain decisions—so you can tune policies to your needs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › GSLB Algorithms
Common GSLB algorithms
Geo-location (GeoDNS)
Routes based on inferred client geography to the nearest region.
Latency-based
Uses measured latency to pick the fastest region for the client.
Weighted routing
Allocates traffic proportionally according to configured weights.
Failover routing
Switches traffic to secondary regions when primaries fail health checks.
IP-based routing
Routes specific IP ranges to chosen regions for partners or internal networks.
Choosing an algorithm
Match the algorithm to your primary objective: latency-sensitive apps often use latency routing; regional compliance or simple locality may use GeoDNS. Combine approaches when necessary for best results.

screens.title: Geo-location-based Routing (GeoDNS)
screens.narratorSegment: Geo-location-based routing uses the client resolver’s IP address to guess the client’s geographic region and routes them to a nearby data center. This approach works well when geographic proximity correlates with lower latency and regulatory boundaries. For example, a user whose resolver is in Germany would typically be directed to European servers, reducing hops and improving page load times. However, the mapping from IP to geography is an approximation: some resolvers are shared by clients in many locations, and undersea cables or peering relationships can make a geographically closer region slower in practice. A misconception is to think GeoDNS guarantees lowest latency; it optimizes for a likely shorter geographic path but cannot see real-time network conditions. Operationally, GeoDNS is easy to reason about and simple to implement, but you should combine it with health checks and consider latency telemetry if performance is critical. Also plan for clients behind corporate proxies or CDNs where the resolver IP does not reflect the true client location. GeoDNS is a strong first step for locality, but not the final word for latency-sensitive services. In practical terms, how inferred client geography routes users to nearby regions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › GeoDNS
Geo-location routing explained
GSLB infers client location from the resolver IP and returns a nearby region to reduce latency.
Use case

Content that benefits from geographic locality, compliance boundaries, or region-specific content distribution.

Limitations
  • Resolver IP may not reflect true client location.
  • Network routing can make a nearby region slower than a farther one.
Concrete example
European users map to EU data centers via GeoDNS, improving directness and often reducing latency compared with routing them to a US region.
Pro tip

Combine GeoDNS with latency sampling or allow overrides for specific IP ranges when true latency measurements show different optimal paths.

screens.title: Latency-based Routing
screens.narratorSegment: Latency-based routing directs clients to the region that can serve them with the lowest observed network latency. This method depends on continuous or recent measurements between GSLB nodes and regional entry points. For instance, a GSLB may maintain historical and real-time ping or synthetic request timings from many vantage points to each data center, and then choose the region that consistently offers the best response time for the client's resolver. This approach can outperform GeoDNS because physical distance does not always predict network performance; routing, congestion, or peering arrangements can make a farther site faster. A concrete example is when a European client is routed to a US-east datacenter because peering provides lower latency despite greater distance; latency routing adapts to that reality. Misconceptions include expecting perfect per-client latency measurement: GSLB typically measures from its vantage points and uses estimates for the client. Also, latency routing requires more operational telemetry and complexity. When low latency is the primary SLA, latency-based routing is often the right strategy, but ensure health checks and fallback policies are in place because routing decisions should avoid unhealthy regions even if they show lower latency briefly.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Latency-based Routing
Latency-based routing
Choose the region with the lowest measured network latency from representative vantage points.
How measurements work

GSLB nodes run synthetic checks and aggregate latency to each region, then use this telemetry to estimate the best mapping for incoming queries.

Practical trade-offs
  • Requires ongoing telemetry and more complex logic.
  • May need smoothing to avoid flapping on transient spikes.
Key Takeaway

Latency routing aims for the fastest real-world path, but requires telemetry and robust health checks to avoid directing traffic to transiently fast but unhealthy regions.

screens.title: Weighted and Failover Routing
screens.narratorSegment: Weighted routing and failover are complementary GSLB strategies for capacity management and disaster recovery. Weighted routing allows operators to assign proportions of traffic to specific regions. For example, if you have a larger US-east cluster and a smaller EU cluster, you can weight traffic 70/30 to reflect capacity, or use weights to perform gradual rollouts and A/B tests. A concrete use case is shifting 10% of traffic to a canary region during a release. Failover routing, in contrast, defines primary and secondary regions. If the GSLB detects the primary is unhealthy through distributed health checks, it redirects traffic to the secondary. This protects against catastrophic primary failures but depends heavily on fast and reliable health detection. A common misconception is to treat weight and failover as independent: in practice you might combine them—weights route traffic under normal operation while failover triggers a full switch when health checks fail. Operationally, ensure health checks are representative, set TTL thinking about cache lifetime during failover, and prepare the application for receiving sudden traffic shifts. Designing sessions and data replication to tolerate these shifts completes the strategy.

keyIdea.text: Weights control steady-state traffic distribution; failover guarantees continuity when a primary region becomes unhealthy. Use both for capacity and resilience.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Weighted & Failover
Weighted routing
Split traffic according to configured weights to reflect capacity or run experiments.
Example

Route 70% to US-east and 30% to EU-west during normal operation, and shift weights during maintenance.

Failover routing
Define primary and backup regions and route all traffic to backup when primary health checks fail.
Operational note

Set robust health checks and consider TTL so cached responses don't delay failover effectiveness.

Why combine them

Use weights for steady traffic management and failover to protect against region outages. Together they provide controlled capacity allocation plus resilience when things go wrong.

screens.title: How GSLB actually routes a DNS query
screens.narratorSegment: When a user requests your domain, the DNS query path determines where GSLB inserts its logic. First, the client asks its local DNS resolver to resolve the domain. That resolver then contacts the authoritative DNS, where GSLB logic runs. The GSLB will inspect the resolver's IP to infer location, consult distributed health checks to ensure data centers are healthy, consult latency or weight configurations, and then return the IP of the chosen regional load balancer. That regional load balancer handles per-request distribution to application servers inside the region. A concrete example: a mobile client in Asia uses its ISP resolver, which queries the authoritative GSLB. The GSLB sees that Asia region is healthy and has low latency metrics, and returns the Asia region's load balancer IP. The client opens a connection to that IP and the regional balancer routes it to an application instance. Misconceptions often arise around who performs health checks: GSLB vendors perform distributed checks rather than the resolver. Also, remember that caching can delay GSLB policy changes, so low TTLs and careful capacity planning are necessary when failover speed is critical.

keyIdea.title: Routing flow
keyIdea.text: GSLB sits at the authoritative DNS and returns an IP for the most appropriate regional load balancer after checking location, health, latency, and policy.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › GSLB routing flow
Control flow
  1. Client asks local resolver to resolve the domain.
  2. Resolver queries authoritative DNS where GSLB logic runs.
  3. GSLB evaluates client location, health, latency, and weights.
  4. GSLB returns the chosen regional load balancer IP.
  5. Client connects to the regional balancer, which forwards to application servers.
Key responsibilities

GSLB handles decision making; regional load balancers handle intra-region traffic distribution and session affinity if needed.

Concrete example

A mobile user in Asia gets the Asia LB IP because health checks and latency metrics favor that region. The LB then forwards the request to a healthy application instance.

Operational note

Set TTLs with awareness of cache propagation and configure health checks that reflect real application readiness.

screens.title: Challenges: TTL, health checks, and multi-region application design
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing GSLB requires careful attention to operational details. DNS caching means that even when the GSLB makes correct decisions, those decisions may not be seen globally until cached records expire. To reduce this effect, providers recommend low TTLs—like 60 seconds—but that increases the volume of DNS queries and the load on authoritative servers. Robust distributed health checks are essential: they must be frequent, representative, and target the full request path, not just a single TCP accept. Additionally, your application must be designed for multi-region operation: data replication strategies or eventual consistency models are required so different regions can serve users without data loss. Session handling is another concern; prefer stateless services or centralized/session-replication strategies to avoid user disruption across regions. Cost and complexity rise as you add regions and manage cross-region data. A common error is to enable GSLB without ensuring the app can handle regional failover—this leads to redirected traffic that cannot be served correctly. Plan for monitoring, capacity, and a gradual rollout so failure modes are visible and manageable before full production traffic is routed globally. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Challenges & Considerations
Key challenges
TTL and caching
Low TTLs speed propagation but increase DNS query load on authoritative servers.
Health checks
Distributed, application-level checks are required to avoid false positives or negatives about region health.
Application design
Ensure statelessness, session strategies, and data replication to handle cross-region traffic shifts.
Cost & complexity
Multiple regions and frequent DNS updates increase operational cost and management overhead.
Actionable checklist

Before enabling GSLB: verify app multi-region readiness, design comprehensive health checks, choose sensible TTLs for your risk tolerance, and plan for additional DNS query capacity.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, DNS is a distributed naming system that maps domain names to IP addresses and can publish multiple IPs, but it does not perform active health checks. Second, Round Robin DNS provides simple distribution but is limited by caching and lack of health awareness. Third, Global Server Load Balancing transforms authoritative DNS into a decision engine that can route traffic using geo-location, latency, weights, or failover rules. You should also remember that TTL determines how quickly DNS changes propagate and that lowering TTLs speeds failover at the cost of more DNS queries. Finally, GSLB is only part of the solution: applications must be designed for multi-region operation, with replication and stateless patterns to accept redirected traffic. Keep these points in mind when evaluating routing policies and operational plans for global services. Which of these concepts will most affect your next multi-region design decision?

Hierarchical name-to-IP mapping service; foundation for routing decisions.
GSLB
Intelligent authoritative DNS that selects the best regional endpoint per query.
TTL
Time To Live controls cache duration; lower TTLs speed propagation but increase DNS query load.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll explore how the Domain Name System, the internet’s phonebook, becomes a decision point for global traffic. DNS starts as a simple mechanism to convert a human name into an IP address. When applications scale across regions, DNS can no longer remain static: we need Global Server Load Balancing, or GSLB, to route users to the best region based on location, latency, health, and capacity. You will learn why Round Robin DNS is insufficient for resilient, low-latency systems, and how GSLB algorithms like geo-location routing, latency-based routing, weighted routing, and failover behave in real deployments. We’ll also examine operational constraints: DNS caching, TTL tuning, and the importance of distributed health checks and multi-region application design. Through concrete examples and a small hands-on DNS zone fragment, you’ll see how a short TTL helps failover but increases DNS load, and why applications must be built to tolerate eventual consistency across regions. By the end, you should understand when GSLB is appropriate, what decisions it can automate, and what trade-offs remain for engineering teams. Consider how the system should behave if a whole region fails — that question will guide many design choices here.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain DNS’s role as the name-to-IP mapping service and recognize its original, limited role in traffic distribution. You should identify why simple techniques like Round Robin are insufficient for modern multi-region systems, including the lack of health checks and the problem of caching. You will also be able to define Global Server Load Balancing and list its common algorithms — geo-location routing, latency-based routing, weighted routing, and failover — and explain when each is appropriate. Finally, you will understand operational constraints such as TTL tuning, distributed health checks, and the application design changes required to operate across regions. Each objective ties a practical skill—like writing a conceptual DNS zone file or choosing a routing algorithm—to a reason why it matters in production. You will practice interpreting TTL trade-offs and plan for failover scenarios, which prepares you to make resilient architecture choices for global services.

These additional objectives focus on practical operation. You will learn to compare specific GSLB algorithms and choose the one that matches a use case, for instance preferring latency-based routing for a global gaming service. You will understand DNS caching mechanics and how TTL affects propagation during failover, illustrated by a short example where changing TTL from one hour to one minute dramatically reduces the delay before clients see an updated IP. Finally, you will be able to list infrastructure prerequisites for GSLB: distributed health checks, low-latency monitoring, and application-level designs such as stateless services or global data replication patterns. The hands-on task included in the chapter guides you to write a conceptual DNS zone file snippet and reason about TTL impact—skills you can apply when planning real deployments or interviews where you must justify TTL, health checks, and failover strategy.

DNS is the hierarchical, distributed naming system that maps human-friendly domain names to numeric IP addresses. At the most basic level this mapping enables browsers and clients to find a server on the network. A traditional DNS record, such as an A record, lists the IP address for a domain and can include multiple IPs. That multiplicity is where DNS begins to resemble a simple load distributor: many resolvers will iterate through or rotate the IP list. A concrete example is a website that publishes two A records: one for a US region and one for a European region. A resolver doing Round Robin may hand out each IP in turn. But it’s crucial to understand that DNS itself does not open connections or verify health; it only supplies addresses. A common misconception is to expect DNS to provide instantaneous failover: because DNS responses are cached by resolvers and client systems, changes may take time to propagate. Therefore, while DNS is the first place you can influence where a user connects, it must be paired with monitoring and short TTLs when you need rapid changes. Think of DNS as the control plane that can steer traffic, but not as the runtime monitor that guarantees successful connections.

Round Robin DNS is a simple technique where a domain publishes multiple A records and the DNS resolver returns IPs in a rotating order. This can distribute new clients across several servers or regions, and in small deployments it can provide a primitive form of load sharing. A concrete example is a small service listing two IPs for myapp. com; successive queries may result in alternating addresses. However, in real networks the effectiveness of Round Robin is limited because the resolvers and caching layers can hold answers for the TTL duration, so multiple clients behind the same resolver will receive the same IP for that period. Another important constraint is that DNS lacks active health checks: if one IP becomes unhealthy, DNS will continue to hand it out until records are changed and cached entries expire. A common misconception is that Round Robin balances load evenly across actual user connections; it balances DNS queries, not necessarily TCP sessions or request load. When you design global services, Round Robin can be a quick start, but you must plan for monitoring, short TTLs if you want rapid changes, and a strategy to remove unhealthy endpoints quickly. Consider also client-side retry behavior: clients that fail over may try another IP, but that adds latency and complexity for user experience.

Traditional DNS's simplicity is also the source of its problems for dynamic, global systems. The first limitation is the absence of active health checks: authoritative DNS doesn't monitor the reachability of backend servers, so an IP that routes to a failed service continues to be handed out. A second limitation is pervasive caching: client devices, local resolvers, and intermediate resolvers store DNS answers for the TTL period. This means a change on the authoritative server can take minutes or hours to become effective worldwide if TTLs are large. A third shortcoming is lack of intelligence: vanilla DNS does not know client geography, real network latency, or server load; it simply returns configured addresses. To illustrate the operational impact, imagine a primary region failing during business hours. With high TTLs, many resolvers will still use cached primary IPs for the duration of the TTL, causing prolonged outages for those clients. A common mitigation is to reduce TTL values, but that increases DNS query volume and load on authoritative servers. The trade-offs are fundamental: faster propagation versus higher DNS traffic. Effective global routing requires a smarter control plane that monitors health, measures latency, and makes per-query decisions—this is precisely where GSLB fits in.

Global Server Load Balancing, or GSLB, extends DNS with intelligence and programmability to map clients to the best regional endpoint. A GSLB system acts as the authoritative DNS for your domain but instead of returning a static list of IPs, it makes per-query decisions based on inputs like client geolocation, recent latency measurements, server health, and configured weights. For example, when a client asks for your application's IP, the GSLB inspects the resolver’s source IP to infer location, consults health checks to ensure regions are healthy, and may consult latency metrics to pick the fastest region. The returned IP is typically the address of a regional load balancer rather than an application server, so the regional balancer handles intra-region distribution. A key benefit is that GSLB centralizes global routing logic while still using DNS as the delivery mechanism. A frequent misconception is that GSLB eliminates the need to design your application for multi-region operation; it does not. You still must handle data replication, session handling, and consistency across regions. GSLB simply helps direct traffic in a smarter way that improves latency and availability at the edge.

GSLB implementations commonly support several routing modes, each with different trade-offs. Geo-location-based routing maps client resolvers to the nearest region by IP-derived geography; it's simple and reduces distance-related latency, but it can be fooled by complex network paths. Latency-based routing measures or estimates network latency between clients and regions and routes to the lowest-latency endpoint; this can better reflect actual performance but requires accurate telemetry. Weighted routing assigns proportional traffic to regions based on configured weights, which is useful for capacity control and staged rollouts. Failover routing defines primary and secondary regions so that if a primary becomes unhealthy, traffic moves to the secondary automatically; this is critical for disaster recovery. Finally, IP-based routing maps specific client IP ranges to designated regions, often used for partners or internal networks. For example, a gaming company prioritizing minimal ping might choose latency-based routing, while a company wanting regional compliance controls might prefer geo-location routing. A misconception to avoid is treating these as mutually exclusive; many GSLB systems combine modes—geo for broad guidance and latency for fine-grain decisions—so you can tune policies to your needs.

Geo-location-based routing uses the client resolver’s IP address to guess the client’s geographic region and routes them to a nearby data center. This approach works well when geographic proximity correlates with lower latency and regulatory boundaries. For example, a user whose resolver is in Germany would typically be directed to European servers, reducing hops and improving page load times. However, the mapping from IP to geography is an approximation: some resolvers are shared by clients in many locations, and undersea cables or peering relationships can make a geographically closer region slower in practice. A misconception is to think GeoDNS guarantees lowest latency; it optimizes for a likely shorter geographic path but cannot see real-time network conditions. Operationally, GeoDNS is easy to reason about and simple to implement, but you should combine it with health checks and consider latency telemetry if performance is critical. Also plan for clients behind corporate proxies or CDNs where the resolver IP does not reflect the true client location. GeoDNS is a strong first step for locality, but not the final word for latency-sensitive services. This method depends on continuous or recent measurements between GSLB nodes and regional entry points. Misconceptions include expecting perfect per-client latency measurement: GSLB typically measures from its vantage points and uses estimates for the client. Also, latency routing requires more operational telemetry and complexity.
